summary: Specifies how to use EAP-TLS with TLS 1.3 while staying backwards compatible with existing EAP-TLS implementations. TLS 1.3 brings better security, privacy, and lower latency. Compared with older versions, EAP-TLS 1.3 always provides forward secrecy, does not disclose the peer identity, and requires revocation checking. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how certificate-based EAP-TLS authentication works with TLS 1.3. It sets rules for private identities, key creation, certificate checks, and later resumption.

questions: does eap-tls 1.3 hide the user identity
how long can eap-tls resumption tickets last
subtitle: EAP-TLS uses the TLS 1.3 handshake for certificate-based network access.

tldr.problem: EAP-TLS was specified for earlier TLS versions, and TLS 1.3 changes handshake messages, key derivation, resumption, and privacy behavior.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9190 defines EAP-TLS procedures for TLS 1.3, including protected success signaling, TLS exporter keys, privacy rules, and resumption tickets.
tldr.outcome: EAP-TLS 1.3 requires forward secrecy, privacy, and certificate revocation checks. RFC 9190 updates RFC 5216 and is itself updated by RFC 9965.

today: RFC 9190 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022. It updates RFC 5216 and has itself been updated by RFC 9965.

sections.title: Why EAP-TLS Needs TLS 1.3 Rules
sections.content:
EAP-TLS uses the TLS handshake inside Extensible Authentication Protocol messages to authenticate peers and establish shared keys. Its earlier specification, RFC 5216, was written for TLS 1.0 and 1.1, while TLS 1.3 changes the handshake, key schedule, resumption, and privacy behavior.

RFC 9190 defines those differences while preserving RFC 5216 behavior when an earlier TLS version is negotiated. Implementations limit the maximum TLS version to 1.3 unless an administrator enables a later version.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 changes how a secure connection is negotiated. EAP-TLS therefore needs updated instructions for using that version while retaining earlier rules for older versions.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The EAP server starts the exchange, and the peer sends a TLS ClientHello inside an EAP response. The TLS handshake continues in EAP request and response packets. The server MUST authenticate with a certificate and SHOULD require a peer certificate; pre-shared-key authentication is not allowed except for resumption.

After it processes the peer's Finished message and sends its last handshake message, the server sends TLS application data 0x00 as a protected success indication. The peer replies with an empty EAP-TLS response, and the server sends EAP-Success. TLS early data and post-handshake authentication MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The peer and server exchange TLS handshake messages inside EAP packets. The server signals success only after the handshake is complete and the peer confirms the signal.

sections.title: Hiding the Peer Identity
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 encrypts certificate messages, and EAP-TLS 1.3 always uses privacy without an extra handshake round. A client MUST NOT send its username or another permanent identifier in cleartext in the EAP Identity Response.

The recommended anonymous Network Access Identifier omits the username, for example by using only a realm. The realm may still be visible, and packet sizes can reveal certificate size unless record padding is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The TLS 1.3 handshake hides certificates from passive observers. The peer also avoids sending a permanent username in the clear, though its network realm may remain visible.

sections.title: Deriving EAP Keys
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 replaces the earlier TLS pseudorandom function with HKDF and a different key schedule. EAP-TLS 1.3 derives Key_Material and Method-Id through the TLS exporter, using EAP Type 0x0D as context.

The exporter returns 128 bytes of Key_Material and 64 bytes for Method-Id. The first 64 bytes of Key_Material form the MSK; the next 64 form the EMSK. Implementations request the exact lengths specified, even if they later use only part of the output.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints use the TLS exporter to produce matching EAP key material. They must request the specified output lengths so that the resulting keys agree.

sections.title: Checking Identities and Certificates
sections.content:
The identity in the initial EAP Identity Response is not authenticated by EAP-TLS and MUST NOT determine authorization or accounting. A server can use it to route the request or choose an authentication method.

Peers should validate the server certificate using a trusted root certificate and a configured server name. A peer may use trust on first use if it lacks a trusted root, but the RFC warns that this increases exposure to interception and does not allow a certificate to change without separate validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The initial name a peer sends is not proof of identity. Authorization should rely on authenticated certificate or resumption data, and the peer should verify the server's certificate name.

sections.title: Revocation and Resumption Security
sections.content:
For TLS 1.3, revocation status MUST be checked for every certificate in the chain except the trust anchor. Servers MUST implement OCSP stapling. Peers must also support checking revocation after network access becomes available and SHOULD NOT trust the network before completing that check.

Resumption uses data cached from the original handshake and MUST NOT proceed if that data cannot be retrieved securely. Tickets and PSKs MUST NOT be stored longer than 604800 seconds. Authorization decisions must be reconsidered when the information used for them changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations check whether certificates have been revoked, including after access to the network begins. A resumed connection must use securely saved information and must not keep its ticket longer than the specified limit.
